claims.text: Rust 1.0 was announced on 15 May 2015 by the Rust Core Team. The announcement states that it "combines low-level control over performance with high-level convenience and safety guarantees".

source.title: Announcing Rust 1.0, The Rust Core Team, The Rust Programming Language Blog, 15 May 2015

claims.text: The announcement states that it achieves these goals "without requiring a garbage collector or runtime", which is what allows its libraries to serve as a drop-in substitute for C.

source.title: Announcing Rust 1.0, The Rust Core Team, The Rust Programming Language Blog, 15 May 2015

claims.text: The announcement attributes the language’s distinctiveness to its type system, described as a refinement and codification of best practices drawn from experience with C and C++. It says newcomers can write low-level code without worrying about minor mistakes leading to mysterious crashes, and that experienced developers save time they would otherwise spend debugging.

source.title: Announcing Rust 1.0, The Rust Core Team, The Rust Programming Language Blog, 15 May 2015

claims.text: The release marks a stability commitment: the announcement describes the preceding churn as ended and breaking changes as largely out of scope going forward, alongside a six-week release train.

source.title: Announcing Rust 1.0, The Rust Core Team, The Rust Programming Language Blog, 15 May 2015

claims.text: The language was sponsored by Mozilla, which supported its development in the years before the 1.0 release.

source.title: Rust (programming language): origins and Mozilla sponsorship

beats.broke: memory safety had always been bought with a runtime, and the code that most needs safety — kernels, drivers, engines — is exactly the code that cannot afford one
beats.fix: make ownership part of the type system and check it when compiling, so the safety property is established before the program runs and costs nothing while it does
beats.cost: the checker must be satisfied, so it rejects correct programs it cannot prove correct, and the work moves to the author
beats.interview: what it means for a compiler to reject a program that would have worked
